\section{Introduction}

The Lucas--Penrose argument asserts that, given any consistent formal system $F$ powerful
enough to encode arithmetic, a human mathematician can recognize the truth of the G\"odel
sentence $g_F$---the sentence expressing its own unprovability in $F$---even though $F$
cannot prove $g_F$. Since $F$ was arbitrary, the argument concludes that the mind is not
identical to any fixed formal system. The argument is philosophically contested, chiefly
because it slides between ``for each system there is a truth it misses'' and ``there is a
mind that misses no truth.'' Our aim is not to adjudicate the metaphysics but to isolate
what is genuinely a theorem, state it with minimal hypotheses, and expose its structural
twin in algorithmic information theory.

We organize the mathematics into four layers: (1) Lawvere's fixed-point theorem, the
categorical diagonal; (2) the impossibility results (Cantor, Tarski, Russell, halting);
(3) abstract incompleteness and the Lucas--Penrose gap, with a concrete model; (4) the
counting kernel of Berry and Chaitin. Section~\ref{sec:corr} draws the correspondence
explicit; Section~\ref{sec:disc} discusses interpretation; Section~\ref{sec:future} lists
future directions.

\section{Preliminaries and notation}

We work with the natural numbers $\N = \{0,1,2,\dots\}$. For $y \in \N$ write $\bits(y)$
for the length of the binary representation of $y$ (with $\bits(0)=0$); equivalently
$\bits(y)$ is the least $n$ with $y < 2^n$. The single arithmetic fact we use repeatedly
is
\begin{equation}\tag{BL}\label{eq:bl}
\bits(y) \le n \iff y < 2^n .
\end{equation}
A function $\enc : X \to Y$ is \emph{injective} if $\enc(a)=\enc(b)$ implies $a=b$. A family
$\varphi : A \to (A \to B)$ is \emph{point-surjective} if for every $g : A \to B$ there is
$a$ with $\varphi(a)=g$. A self-map $f : B \to B$ has a \emph{fixed point} if $f(b)=b$ for
some $b$.

\section{Lawvere's fixed-point theorem and the diagonal family}

\begin{theorem}[Lawvere]\label{thm:lawvere}
Let $A,B$ be types and $\varphi : A \to (A \to B)$ be point-surjective. Then every
$f : B \to B$ has a fixed point.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Apply point-surjectivity to $g(x) := f(\varphi(x)(x))$: there is $a$ with $\varphi(a)=g$.
Then $\varphi(a)(a) = g(a) = f(\varphi(a)(a))$, so $b := \varphi(a)(a)$ satisfies
$f(b)=b$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Diagonal lemma]
If $\varphi : A \to (A \to \Prop)$ is point-surjective, then every operator
$f : \Prop \to \Prop$ has a fixed point $p \iff f(p)$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Cantor / Tarski]\label{thm:cantor}
No family $\varphi : A \to (A \to \Prop)$ is point-surjective.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If it were, the diagonal lemma applied to negation would produce $p$ with $p \iff \lnot p$,
a contradiction.
\end{proof}

Read semantically, Theorem~\ref{thm:cantor} is Tarski's undefinability of truth; as a
statement about membership it is Cantor's theorem, and specialized to self-membership it is
Russell's paradox. Over the Booleans it yields the halting-problem core.

\begin{theorem}[No Boolean self-enumeration]\label{thm:halting}
For no type $\alpha$ is a map $\mathrm{enum} : \alpha \to (\alpha \to \mathrm{Bool})$
surjective.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
A surjective $\mathrm{enum}$ is point-surjective, so Theorem~\ref{thm:lawvere} gives a fixed
point of Boolean negation, which has none.
\end{proof}

\section{Abstract incompleteness and the Lucas--Penrose gap}

\begin{definition}[Formal system]\label{def:fs}
A \emph{formal system} consists of a type $S$ of \textbf{sentences}; a \textbf{provability}
predicate $\Prov : S \to \Prop$; a \textbf{negation} $\lnot(\cdot) : S \to S$; a
\textbf{truth valuation} $T : S \to \Prop$; and a distinguished \textbf{G\"odel sentence}
$g \in S$, subject to
\begin{itemize}
\item[(neg)] $T(\lnot s) \iff \lnot\, T(s)$ for all $s$;
\item[(snd)] $\Prov(s) \Rightarrow T(s)$ for all $s$ \quad(\textbf{soundness});
\item[(fix)] $T(g) \iff \lnot\,\Prov(g)$.
\end{itemize}
\end{definition}

We read $T$ as ``the mind'' and $\Prov$ as ``the machine.'' Condition (fix) is the single
fixed point the diagonal construction delivers; we do \emph{not} assume a total
self-referential operator giving $T(\mathrm{diag}\,\psi) \iff \psi(\mathrm{diag}\,\psi)$ for
every $\psi$, which is inconsistent (take $\psi = \lnot$, the Liar).

\begin{theorem}[G\"odel unprovability]\label{thm:gunprov}
$\lnot\,\Prov(g)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $\Prov(g)$, then (snd) gives $T(g)$, and (fix) turns $T(g)$ into $\lnot\,\Prov(g)$, a
contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The mind sees the truth]\label{thm:gtrue}
$T(g)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:gunprov}, $\lnot\,\Prov(g)$; apply (fix).
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Negation unprovable]
$\lnot\,\Prov(\lnot g)$; hence $g$ is independent.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $\Prov(\lnot g)$, then (snd) gives $T(\lnot g)$ and (neg) gives $\lnot\, T(g)$,
contradicting Theorem~\ref{thm:gtrue}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Incompleteness / Lucas--Penrose]\label{thm:incomplete}
It is not the case that every true sentence is provable:
$\lnot\big(\forall s,\ T(s) \Rightarrow \Prov(s)\big)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Such a rule applied to $g$ would give $\Prov(g)$ from $T(g)$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:gtrue}),
contradicting Theorem~\ref{thm:gunprov}.
\end{proof}

Combining Theorems~\ref{thm:gunprov} and~\ref{thm:gtrue} gives the \textbf{mind/machine
gap}: $T(g) \wedge \lnot\,\Prov(g)$.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Interpretation.} Theorem~\ref{thm:incomplete} is the defensible kernel of
Lucas--Penrose: no single sound self-referential system is complete for its own truths. It
does not assert that no machine can ever recognize $g$; a strictly larger system that
adjoins $g$ as an axiom proves it (and has its own fresh G\"odel sentence). Whether a human
mind is more than some fixed such system is exactly what the theorem leaves open.

\begin{proposition}[Non-vacuity]
Let $S = \mathrm{Bool}$, $T(b) := (b = \mathrm{true})$, $\lnot(\cdot) := \mathrm{not}$,
$\Prov(\cdot) := \bot$, and $g := \mathrm{true}$. This is a sound formal system in which
$T(g) \wedge \lnot\,\Prov(g)$ holds.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
(neg) and (fix) are checked by cases on the Boolean; (snd) holds vacuously since $\Prov$ is
everywhere false. The gap is then Theorems~\ref{thm:gunprov}--\ref{thm:gtrue}.
\end{proof}

Soundness is load-bearing: without it Theorem~\ref{thm:incomplete} fails, since a system
that proves everything is complete but unsound.

\section{The counting kernel: Berry and Chaitin}

Fix an \emph{injective} encoding $\enc : \N \to \N$; think of $\enc(x)$ as the unique code
of $x$. Define the \textbf{descriptive complexity}
\[
K(x) := \bits(\enc(x)),
\]
the number of binary digits of the code of $x$. By~\eqref{eq:bl}, $K(x) \le n \iff \enc(x)
< 2^n$.

\begin{theorem}[Finite Berry pigeonhole]\label{thm:berry}
For every $n$, among the $2^n+1$ numbers $0,1,\dots,2^n$ there is at least one $x$ with
$K(x) > n$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Suppose $K(x) \le n$, i.e.\ $\enc(x) < 2^n$, for all $x \in \{0,\dots,2^n\}$. Then $\enc$
maps this $(2^n{+}1)$-element set injectively into $\{0,\dots,2^n-1\}$, of size $2^n$; the
image has $2^n+1$ elements yet lies in a set of size $2^n$, and $2^n+1 \le 2^n$ is absurd.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Chaitin incompressibility]\label{thm:chaitin}
For every threshold $n$ there is $x$ with $K(x) > n$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $K(x) \le n$ for all $x$, then $x \mapsto \enc(x)$ injects the infinite set $\N$ into the
finite set $\{0,\dots,2^n-1\}$, forcing $\N$ to be finite---a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Infinitely many incompressibles]\label{thm:inf}
For every $n$, the set $\{x : K(x) > n\}$ is infinite.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The compressible set $\{x : K(x) \le n\} = \enc^{-1}(\{y : y < 2^n\})$ is the preimage under
the injective $\enc$ of a finite set, hence finite; its complement is infinite.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[No universal compressor]
There is no global bound $B$ with $K(x) < B$ for all $x$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Given $B$, Theorem~\ref{thm:chaitin} supplies $x$ with $K(x) > B$, contradicting $K(x)<B$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Constructive Berry paradox]
For every $n$, the set $\{x : K(x) > n\}$ is nonempty, so ``the least number of complexity
greater than $n$'' always denotes a genuine object. That description is itself short---of
length roughly $\log n$ plus a constant---yet names an object of complexity $>n$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Nonemptiness is Theorem~\ref{thm:chaitin}.
\end{proof}

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Necessity of injectivity.} The identity encoding $\enc = \mathrm{id}$ is
injective, so Theorems~\ref{thm:berry}--\ref{thm:inf} have genuine content. Dropping
injectivity destroys them: the constant code $\enc(x)=0$ has $K(x)=0$ for all $x$.

\section{The correspondence}\label{sec:corr}

The two axes are the same theorem in different coordinates:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ll}
\hline
Logical axis & Information axis \\
\hline
provability $\Prov$ & compressibility $K(x) \le n$ \\
true but unprovable $g$ & incompressible number $x$ \\
$T(g) \wedge \lnot\Prov(g)$ & $K(x) > n$ \\
proved by fixed-point diagonal & proved by pigeonhole / cardinality \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
In both cases a finitely specified apparatus tries to cover an infinite domain and provably
leaves a witness uncovered. Theorem~\ref{thm:gtrue} (``some truth is unprovable'') is the
exact analogue of Theorem~\ref{thm:chaitin} (``some number is incompressible''). Both, with
the halting problem (Theorem~\ref{thm:halting}), are specializations of
Theorem~\ref{thm:lawvere}: \emph{a finitely described mirror of an infinite domain must
omit something from its reflection.}

\section{Applications and interpretation}\label{sec:disc}

\textbf{Philosophy of mind.} What is provable is the relative claim
(Theorem~\ref{thm:incomplete}): every fixed sound self-referential system has a blind spot.
What is not established is that a human mind certifies all truths; the counter-move---that
the mind is itself some fixed system whose blind spot it has not located---is untouched.

\textbf{Algorithmic information theory.} Theorems~\ref{thm:berry}--\ref{thm:inf} are the
combinatorial heart of Kolmogorov--Chaitin complexity: most objects are incompressible, and
incompressibility drives the incompressibility method for lower bounds.

\textbf{Logic and computability.} Section~3 packages Cantor, Russell, Tarski, and the
halting problem as instances of one theorem.

\section{Future directions}\label{sec:future}

\textbf{A quantitative Lucas--Penrose gap.} For every sound self-referential system there
should be a strictly increasing hierarchy of independent truths: adjoining the G\"odel
sentence yields a larger sound system with its own fresh G\"odel sentence, and the ordinal
length of this reflection tower is an invariant of the system.

\textbf{Complexity-graded incompleteness.} In any sound system expressing its own
descriptive-complexity bounds, the largest provable lower bound ``$K(x)>c$'' should be
bounded by a constant fixed by the system's own description length and computable from its
G\"odel sentence.

\textbf{Berry as a resource lower bound.} The finite Berry pigeonhole should sharpen to a
smooth trade-off: any encoding keeping average code length below $n-k$ must fail injectivity
on a set of size at least $2^k$, with the constant tight.

\section{Conclusion}

Stripped to essentials, ``mind vs.\ G\"odel'' is a statement about the reach of finite
descriptions. Lawvere's fixed-point theorem generates a diagonal that, on the logical axis,
produces a true-but-unprovable sentence and, on the information axis, an incompressible
number reachable by pure counting. The defensible Lucas--Penrose kernel is precisely the
relative incompleteness of any fixed sound self-referential system, and its twin in
algorithmic information theory shows the same limitation is a law of finite description.

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Callable, List


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Descriptive complexity
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def bits(y: int) -> int:
    """Number of binary digits of y (bits(0) = 0). This is the least n with y < 2^n."""
    return y.bit_length()


def K(enc: Callable[[int], int], x: int) -> int:
    """Descriptive complexity of x relative to an encoding enc: bit-length of its code."""
    return bits(enc(x))


def size_le_iff_lt_pow(y: int, n: int) -> bool:
    """Verify the load-bearing arithmetic fact  bits(y) <= n  <=>  y < 2^n."""
    return (bits(y) <= n) == (y < 2 ** n)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Finite Berry pigeonhole
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def berry_witness(enc: Callable[[int], int], n: int) -> int:
    """
    Return a witness x in {0, ..., 2^n} with K(x) > n, guaranteed to exist for any
    INJECTIVE enc by the finite Berry pigeonhole (Theorem 5.1).
    """
    for x in range(2 ** n + 1):
        if K(enc, x) > n:
            return x
    raise AssertionError("no witness found: encoding is not injective on this range")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Chaitin incompressibility (search for a witness above threshold n)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def chaitin_witness(enc: Callable[[int], int], n: int, search_limit: int = 10 ** 6) -> int:
    """
    Return the least x found with K(x) > n. For an injective enc such an x must exist
    (Theorem 5.2); we scan up to search_limit as a practical bound.
    """
    for x in range(search_limit):
        if K(enc, x) > n:
            return x
    raise AssertionError("no incompressible witness within search_limit")


def count_incompressible(enc: Callable[[int], int], n: int, upto: int) -> int:
    """Count x in [0, upto) with K(x) > n; illustrates that incompressibles are dense."""
    return sum(1 for x in range(upto) if K(enc, x) > n)

class FormalSystem:

      - Prov(b)   : the "machine" (mechanical derivation relation)
      - neg       : syntactic negation
      - godel     : the distinguished Gödel sentence with  True_(g) <=> not Prov(g)

    """

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.godel: bool = True

    def true_(self, b: bool) -> bool:
        return b is True

    def prov(self, b: bool) -> bool:
        return False  # the machine proves nothing -> trivially sound

    def neg(self, b: bool) -> bool:
        return not b

    def mind_outstrips_machine(self) -> bool:
        """Return True iff the Gödel sentence is true but unprovable."""
        return self.true_(self.godel) and not self.prov(self.godel)

We model an observer watching a dynamic social network whose instantaneous
configuration ranges over a finite state space `S` (for example, the set of all
adjacency relations the network may exhibit at a given instant).  The observer
records a measurement drawn from an alphabet `M` through an *observation channel*
`obs : S → M`, and later attempts to reconstruct the true configuration with a
*decoder* `dec : M → S`.

Two idealized regimes are of interest:

* **Perfect surveillance** — the channel is injective, so the true configuration
  is always recoverable from the record.
* **Perfect privacy** — the channel is constant, so the record reveals nothing
  about the configuration.

/-- Perfect surveillance is achievable exactly when the record alphabet is at
least as large as the state space; the counting bound is therefore tight. -/
theorem exists_surveillance_iff :
    (∃ obs : S → M, PerfectSurveillance obs) ↔ Fintype.card S ≤ Fintype.card M := by
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨obs, hobs⟩
    exact Fintype.card_le_of_injective obs hobs
  · intro h
    obtain ⟨e⟩ := Function.Embedding.nonempty_of_card_le h
    exact ⟨e, e.injective⟩

omit [Fintype S] [Fintype M] [DecidableEq S] [DecidableEq M] in
/-- Perfect privacy is always available whenever the record alphabet is nonempty. -/
theorem exists_privacy [Nonempty M] : ∃ obs : S → M, PerfectPrivacy obs :=
  ⟨fun _ => Classical.arbitrary M, fun _ _ => rfl⟩

/-! ### The rate–distortion covering bound -/

omit [Fintype M] [DecidableEq S] in
/-- **Rate–distortion lower bound.**  Fix a dissimilarity `d` on configurations, a
distortion budget `D`, and a bound `B` on the size of every distortion ball
`{s | d c s ≤ D}`.  If the observer reconstructs every configuration to within
`D`, then the channel must emit at least `|S| / B` distinct records:
`|S| ≤ rate · B`. -/
theorem covering_rate_bound (obs : S → M) (dec : M → S) (d : S → S → ℕ) (D B : ℕ)
    (hball : ∀ c : S, (Finset.univ.filter (fun s => d c s ≤ D)).card ≤ B)
    (hrec : ∀ s, d (dec (obs s)) s ≤ D) :
    Fintype.card S ≤ rate obs * B := by
  have hpart : (Finset.univ : Finset S).card
      = ∑ m ∈ Finset.univ.image obs, (Finset.univ.filter (fun s => obs s = m)).card := by
    apply Finset.card_eq_sum_card_fiberwise
    intro x _
    exact Finset.mem_image_of_mem obs (Finset.mem_univ x)
  rw [Fintype.card, hpart, rate]
  calc ∑ m ∈ Finset.univ.image obs, (Finset.univ.filter (fun s => obs s = m)).card
      ≤ ∑ _m ∈ Finset.univ.image obs, B := by
        apply Finset.sum_le_sum
        intro m _
        refine le_trans (Finset.card_le_card ?_) (hball (dec m))
        intro s hs
        simp only [Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_univ, true_and] at hs ⊢
        rw [← hs]
        exact hrec s
    _ = (Finset.univ.image obs).card * B := by rw [Finset.sum_const]; ring

/-! ### Perfect privacy: the `rate = 1` corner and its impossibilities -/

omit [Fintype M] [DecidableEq S] in
/-- A perfectly private channel has rate exactly `1`: it emits a single record. -/
theorem rate_eq_one_of_privacy [Nonempty S] {obs : S → M} (hp : PerfectPrivacy obs) :
    rate obs = 1 := by
  rw [rate, Finset.card_eq_one]
  refine ⟨obs (Classical.arbitrary S), ?_⟩
  apply Finset.eq_singleton_iff_unique_mem.2
  refine ⟨Finset.mem_image_of_mem obs (Finset.mem_univ _), ?_⟩
  intro x hx
  simp only [Finset.mem_image, Finset.mem_univ, true_and] at hx
  obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ := hx
  rw [← ha]
  exact hp a _

omit [Fintype M] [DecidableEq S] in
/-- **Privacy versus distortion.**  A perfectly private observer can meet the
distortion budget `D` only if a single distortion ball already covers the entire
network: `|S| ≤ B`.  Thus privacy is compatible with fidelity only when the
network is intrinsically indistinguishable at scale `D`. -/
theorem privacy_forces_ball_cover [Nonempty S] (obs : S → M) (dec : M → S)
    (d : S → S → ℕ) (D B : ℕ)
    (hball : ∀ c : S, (Finset.univ.filter (fun s => d c s ≤ D)).card ≤ B)
    (hp : PerfectPrivacy obs) (hrec : ∀ s, d (dec (obs s)) s ≤ D) :
    Fintype.card S ≤ B := by
  have h := covering_rate_bound obs dec d D B hball hrec
  rw [rate_eq_one_of_privacy hp, one_mul] at h
  exact h

omit [Fintype M] [DecidableEq S] [DecidableEq M] in
/-- **Perfect privacy forbids faithful reconstruction** of a non-trivial network:
if the network has at least two configurations, no decoder can recover a perfectly
private channel. -/
theorem privacy_no_recon {obs : S → M} {dec : M → S} (h2 : 2 ≤ Fintype.card S)
    (hp : PerfectPrivacy obs) : ¬ PerfectReconstruction obs dec := by
  intro hr
  have hinj := recon_inj hr
  obtain ⟨s, t, hst⟩ := Fintype.exists_pair_of_one_lt_card (α := S) (by omega)
  exact hst (hinj (hp s t))

omit [Fintype M] [DecidableEq S] [DecidableEq M] in
/-- **Perfect surveillance and perfect privacy are mutually exclusive** on any
finite network with at least two configurations. -/
theorem privacy_surv_exclusive {obs : S → M} (h2 : 2 ≤ Fintype.card S) :
    ¬ (PerfectPrivacy obs ∧ PerfectSurveillance obs) := by
  rintro ⟨hp, hs⟩
  obtain ⟨s, t, hst⟩ := Fintype.exists_pair_of_one_lt_card (α := S) (by omega)
  exact hst (hs (hp s t))

omit [Fintype M] [DecidableEq S] [DecidableEq M] in
/-- Contrapositive summary: on a non-trivial network a channel achieving perfect
surveillance necessarily leaks — it cannot be perfectly private. -/
theorem surv_leaks {obs : S → M} (h2 : 2 ≤ Fintype.card S)
    (hs : PerfectSurveillance obs) : ¬ PerfectPrivacy obs := by
  intro hp
  exact privacy_surv_exclusive h2 ⟨hp, hs⟩

/-! ### Concrete instantiation: directed social networks on `n` nodes

A snapshot of a directed social network on `n` participants is an adjacency
relation `Fin n → Fin n → Bool`.  There are exactly `2 ^ (n * n)` such snapshots,
so the abstract bounds above specialize to concrete bit counts. -/

/-- The number of directed network snapshots on `n` nodes is `2 ^ (n * n)`. -/
theorem card_directed_network (n : ℕ) :
    Fintype.card (Fin n → Fin n → Bool) = 2 ^ (n * n) := by
  simp [Fintype.card_bool, Fintype.card_fin]
  ring

/-- **Reconstructing a directed network costs `n²` bits.**  Any observer that can
exactly reconstruct every directed social network on `n` nodes must collect at
least `n * n` bits of information. -/
theorem directed_network_bits {M : Type*} [Fintype M] {n : ℕ}
    (obs : (Fin n → Fin n → Bool) → M) (dec : M → (Fin n → Fin n → Bool))
    (h : PerfectReconstruction obs dec) :
    n * n ≤ Nat.log 2 (Fintype.card M) := by
  have hb := recon_bits h
  rw [card_directed_network, Nat.log_pow (b := 2) (by norm_num)] at hb
  exact hb

/-- On any network with at least one node the snapshot space is non-trivial, so
perfect privacy and perfect surveillance cannot coexist there either. -/
theorem directed_network_privacy_surv_exclusive {M : Type*} [Fintype M] {n : ℕ}
    (hn : 1 ≤ n) (obs : (Fin n → Fin n → Bool) → M) :
    ¬ (PerfectPrivacy obs ∧ PerfectSurveillance obs) := by
  apply privacy_surv_exclusive
  rw [card_directed_network]
  have : 1 ≤ n * n := Nat.mul_pos hn hn
  calc 2 = 2 ^ 1 := by norm_num
    _ ≤ 2 ^ (n * n) := Nat.pow_le_pow_right (by norm_num) this

# Computational Evidence — Information-Theoretic Undetectability of Surveillance

We record the small-case computations that motivated the theorems in
`RateDistortion.lean`.

## 1. Counting the configuration space

A directed social network on `n` nodes is an adjacency relation
`Fin n → Fin n → Bool`, so the number of instantaneous configurations is

| n | # configurations = 2^(n·n) | bits = n·n |
|---|-----------------------------|------------|
| 1 | 2                           | 1          |
| 2 | 16                          | 4          |
| 3 | 512                         | 9          |
| 4 | 65536                       | 16         |
| 5 | 33 554 432                  | 25         |

The bit count `n²` is exactly `log₂` of the configuration count, confirming the
prediction of the reconstruction bound `directed_network_bits`.

## 2. Perfect reconstruction forces an injective channel

For `n = 1` there are two configurations (the self-loop present or absent). An
observation channel `obs` into an alphabet of size `1` cannot separate them, so
no decoder recovers the network — matching `privacy_no_recon`. With an alphabet
of size `2`, the identity channel reconstructs perfectly, matching the tightness
statement `exists_surveillance_iff` (`|S| ≤ |M|`).

## 3. Rate–distortion covering, sampled

Take the Hamming dissimilarity `d(x,y) = #{edges where x, y differ}` on the
`n = 2` network space (`|S| = 16`).

* Distortion budget `D = 0`: every ball is a single point (`B = 1`), so the
  covering bound gives `rate ≥ 16` — perfect surveillance.
* Distortion budget `D = 1`: each ball (a configuration together with its
  single-edge neighbours) has `B = 1 + 4 = 5`, so `rate ≥ ⌈16/5⌉ = 4`.
* Distortion budget `D = 4`: one ball already covers all `16` configurations
  (`B = 16`), so `rate ≥ 1` — perfect privacy becomes feasible.

This is precisely the `rate = 1` corner isolated by `privacy_forces_ball_cover`:
a private observer can meet a distortion budget only once a single ball swallows
the whole network.

## 4. Counterexample hunt

We searched for a channel on a two-configuration network that is simultaneously
constant (perfectly private) and injective (perfectly surveilling). None exists:
a constant map identifies the two configurations while an injective map separates
them, a direct contradiction. This is the finite-network mutual-exclusivity
theorem `privacy_surv_exclusive`, and no counterexample was found for any tested
`n ≥ 1`.

# Future Directions — Surveillance Networks and the Privacy–Utility Frontier

The results of this cycle establish a hard covering inequality linking an
observer's channel rate to the distortion at which a finite dynamic network can
be reconstructed, and pin perfect privacy to the degenerate `rate = 1` corner of
that inequality. The following conjectures push the frontier outward.

## Conjecture 1 — A logarithmic rate–distortion staircase

For a network on `n` nodes under the edge-Hamming dissimilarity, the minimum
channel rate needed to reconstruct within distortion `D` equals
`2^(n² − f(n, D))`, where `f(n, D)` is the log-size of a Hamming ball of radius
`D` in dimension `n²`, and the achievable rates form a strictly decreasing
staircase in `D`.

The key insight is that the fibrewise covering argument is tight whenever the
distortion balls tile the configuration space, so the extremal channel is a
perfect covering code and the rate is governed entirely by ball volume.

Why now? The covering lower bound is already in hand; the remaining step is a
matching construction, and covering-code volume estimates in the Hamming cube are
exactly the tool needed to close the gap.

## Conjecture 2 — Privacy is monotone in temporal aggregation

If an observer aggregates snapshots over a time window of length `T` before
reporting, the achievable privacy (largest distortion ball that still permits
`rate = 1`) grows at least linearly in `T`, so temporal blurring is a provably
optimal privacy mechanism up to a constant factor.

The key insight is that aggregation is a channel composition, and composing a
private channel with any post-processing cannot decrease privacy, while a
window-average enlarges the indistinguishability ball at a controlled rate.

Why now? The single-snapshot `rate = 1` characterization gives the base case;
extending it to composed channels only requires a data-processing style
inequality for the covering functional developed here.

## Conjecture 3 — Sparse networks are cheaper to surveil but harder to hide

Restricting to networks with at most `k` edges reduces the reconstruction cost
from `n²` bits to `Θ(k log(n²/k))` bits, yet simultaneously shrinks every
distortion ball, so the privacy threshold `B` collapses and perfect privacy
becomes unattainable for `k ≥ 1` once `n` is large.

The key insight is that sparsity trades configuration-space volume for ball
volume asymmetrically: the numerator of the covering bound shrinks faster than
the denominator, tightening the privacy–utility gap.

Why now? The counting corollary for the full space is settled; the sparse count
is a standard binomial estimate, so the two halves of the covering ratio can be
compared directly.

## Conjecture 4 — A phase transition in observer coalitions

If several independent observers each hold a low-rate channel and later pool
their records, reconstruction fidelity exhibits a sharp threshold: below a
critical total rate the pooled distortion stays macroscopic, and above it the
network is reconstructed almost exactly, with a transition window of width
vanishing in `n`.

The key insight is that pooling multiplies the effective alphabet, so the
covering bound crosses the configuration count abruptly as the summed log-rates
pass `n²`.

Why now? The additivity of `log` rate under channel products follows from the
counting lemma proved this cycle, turning the coalition question into a single
threshold comparison.
